# From Polynesian transcription to Unicode: the journey of Tangaroa

Long before it was a domain, ​this name traveled through scripts. **Tangaroa** begins in Polynesian transcription, passes through scholarly transliteration, and ends — for now — inside the punycode machinery of the global DNS. Each stage of that ‌journey preserves some information and loses some, and the craft of restoration is knowing exactly which marks matter. This post follows the name stage by stage: the original script, the reconstructed pronunciation, ‌the mythological record, the material evidence, and finally the Unicode form that carries all of it into the address bar. Think of it as a biography of a name, told through its ​spelling.

## At a Glance

- **Restored name:** Tangaroa
- **ASCII form:** tangaroa
- **Meaning:** "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)"
- **Domain of influence:** Ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing
- **Pantheon:** Polynesian
- **Restoration:** ASCII-equivalent form

## Overview

**Tangaroa** ​(*tangaroa*) — Ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing · God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa) — belongs to the Polynesian tradition, where it is catalogued under the domain "Ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing". The ​name means "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)".

**Tangaroa** is ocean, sea creatures, fishing. The name means "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)" and belongs to the polynesian tradition.

PuniCodex ​restores the name as **Tangaroa** and serves its temple at [its temple](https://punicodex.com/tangaroa/). The restoration needs no distinctive letters or diacritics its ASCII form would lose. The plain ASCII form *tangaroa* survives as ​a modern convenience imposed by the early domain-name system; the restoration, not the fallback, is the form the project defends as philologically complete.

## The Original Script

No indigenous writing system is securely attested for individual polynesian names. The form shown is a modern scholarly transliteration.

The form ​**Tangaroa** is therefore a scholarly transliteration rather than an attested ancient spelling; it encodes the reconstructed sound of the name for modern use, and no mark in it is decorative.

## Pronunciation

The ‌reconstructed pronunciation of the name is **/tangaroa/** — Restored scholarly form.

Phoneme by phoneme:

- **tangaroa** — The canonical restored form Tangaroa.

For the modern speaker, the closest approximation is: Say "tangaroa" with ​the stress and length implied by the scholarly restoration "Tangaroa".

The ASCII form "tangaroa" is a DNS compromise; the restoration "Tangaroa" preserves the name's scholarly dignity.

The pronunciation given above reconstructs the ​sound world in which Tangaroa was invoked. Modern speakers should not expect exact identity with ancient phonology; the reconstruction is a scholarly compass, not a performance prescription. The restoration Tangaroa keeps the ​prosodic information visible even when the name is typed in plain ASCII.

## Mythology

The stories of Tangaroa place ocean, sea creatures, fishing at the center of a living mythological world.

### Origins (Myth)

​Tangaroa appears in polynesian tradition as ocean, sea creatures, fishing. The name's meaning, "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)", shapes the narratives told about this figure.

### Worship and Memory (Cult)

Devotees ​and later tradition-keepers preserved Tangaroa in ritual, text, and iconography, ensuring the name survived into the modern scholarly record.

The myths of Tangaroa survive in fragments, summaries, and later retellings. Each version ‌reflects the interests of its tellers — poets, priests, philosophers, and scholars. The PuniCodex entry does not privilege a single version; it gathers the attestations so that readers can compare them. ​The restoration Tangaroa gives the figure a stable name around which these variants orbit.

### Born Between the Embrace (Genealogy)

Tangaroa was born into the darkness that lay between Ranginui, the Sky, and ‌Papatūānuku, the Earth, whose embrace left no room and no light for their children. With his brothers Tāne, Tāwhirimātea, Tūmatauenga, Rongo, and Haumia-tiketike he grew to manhood in that cramped twilight, and ​with them he debated how to escape: Tūmatauenga counseled killing the parents outright, Tāne proposed forcing them apart. When Tāne at last pushed Ranginui into the sky and light flooded the world, ‌Tangaroa looked at the dry land his brother had won and chose the other half of creation: **he went down into the ocean, and took it for his own**. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ​ch. 1; Smith, The Lore of the Whare-wānanga.) The myth reads the coastline as a family wound: the sea is not the land's opposite but its brother, still angry.

### The Children Who ‌Split in Two (The Storm War)

Not all the brothers accepted the separation. Tāwhirimātea, the wind, remained with his father in the sky and made war on the others, and Tangaroa's domain ​was his first battlefield: the sea boiled under the storm. In the rout, Tangaroa's grandchildren — the children of his son Punga — **split forever**. Ikatere, father of the fish, fled into ‌the deep and cried 'swim, my children'; Tū-te-wehiwehi, father of the reptiles, scrambled ashore into Tāne's forests and cried 'hide, my children.' Hence the hostility the myth sees everywhere along the tideline: ​fish devour the lizards cast into the sea, and the sea never forgives the land. (Grey, Polynesian Mythology, ch. 1.) What looks like natural enmity is re-read as a family separated under ​fire — every fish a refugee, every lizard a deserter's child.

### Hine-moana, Mother of All That Swim (The Ocean Wife)

In the traditions recorded by Elsdon Best, Tangaroa's wife is **Hine-moana**, 'ocean ‌woman' — not a separate power but the sea itself, personified as the mother of the fish tribes. Every species is their child, which is why the fisherman addresses the sea ‌as kin, and why the first fish of a catch was laid back into the water: a family does not eat its greeting. The canoes that crossed Hine-moana to reach Aotearoa were ‌themselves spoken of as her children, and the rituals of launching, fishing, and beaching observed her tapu; even the nets and lines were named and placated. (Best, Māori Religion and Mythology; Best, ​The Māori as He Was.) The theology is ecological before the word existed: the ocean is not a resource but a marriage, and the catch is a relative arriving for dinner.

## Symbols ​& Iconography

The iconography associated with Tangaroa concentrates in a small set of recurring attributes, each a compressed statement about the name:

- **Name** — The restored form Tangaroa, carrying scholarly and cultural ‌weight.
- **Domain** — Ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing

Symbols function as a visual shorthand: they allow devotees and artists to recognize Tangaroa across media and centuries. The attributes listed above are not decorative; ​each one encodes a claim about power, identity, or function. The restored spelling Tangaroa carries the same precision in textual form.

- **The fish-hook (matau)** — The carved hook with which his descendants ​take his children from the sea — every catch a petition, every offering a repayment.
- **The whale and the shark** — His largest and most feared children; the whale (tohorā) and the ‌shark (mangō) carry his mana in bulk.
- **The canoe (waka)** — The vessel that crosses his domain; canoes were tapu and addressed as kin, because the sea is a relative who must ​be asked.
- **The tide** — Tangaroa-whakamau-tai, 'Tangaroa who fixes the tides' — one of his names, and the rhythm by which fishermen read him.
- **The lizard (ngarara)** — His grandchildren who hid ​ashore: the lizards, fish that chose the land — kin, yet forever on the wrong side of the beach.

## Archaeology & Evidence

No monument, inscription, or artifact in the current PuniCodex corpus ‌is yet assigned to Tangaroa with certainty. That absence should be read honestly: for a Polynesian name of this type the material record is expected to be thin, and the primary ​evidence remains the textual testimony gathered in the Scholarly Sources section.

Were such evidence to surface, it would take recognizable forms: votive or dedicatory inscriptions naming Tangaroa, sanctuary or cult remains tied ‌to ocean and iconography matching its traditional attributes (name and domain). Each candidate would be weighed against the reconstructed form of the name before entering the scholarly record.

## Realm & Domain

**Tangaroa** ​is ocean, sea creatures, fishing. The name means "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)" and belongs to the polynesian tradition.

### Sacred Name

The restoration Tangaroa returns the figure to scholarly recognition.

### ​Ocean

Central domain: ocean, sea creatures, fishing.

### Living Tradition

Honored in polynesian myth, cult, and cultural memory.

### Unicode Restoration

Preserved as a flagship temple despite the unregistrable plain-ASCII form.

### Lord of Ocean

​He took the sea for his domain when his parents were separated, vowing in the recitations never to return to the land.

### Father of Fishes

With Hine-moana, the ocean woman, he is ​ancestor of every finned and swimming creature the nets take.

### The Exiled Brother

Tāwhirimātea's war drove him from the coast; his grandchildren scattered to sea and shore, splitting into fish and lizard.

### ‌One Name, Many Islands

Ta'aroa in Tahiti, Tangaloa in Tonga and Samoa, Kanaloa in Hawai'i — one ocean god under four island names.

## Across Cultures

Cross-cultural identifications are rarely one-to-one. Tangaroa may be likened to figures in neighboring traditions without being identical to ​them. The PuniCodex crosslink index records these resonances as relationships, not equations. The restored form Tangaroa makes such comparisons possible across language boundaries.

## Cultural Legacy

Tangaroa remains a touchstone for understanding polynesian ‌religion, art, and identity.

The modern afterlife of Tangaroa includes scholarly editions, artistic adaptations, and popular references. Each reuse renegotiates the figure’s meaning for a new audience. The PuniCodex temple participates in ​that afterlife by ensuring that the restored name Tangaroa remains findable and citable.

## A Meditation

To contemplate ‌Tangaroa is to hold the idea of ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing in the mind and to ask what of it endures. The name means "God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian *Taŋaroa)" — ‌and a name that carries its meaning so openly invites meditation rather than mere recollection. The tradition remembers the name as ocean, Sea Creatures, Fishing · God of the sea (from Proto-Polynesian ‌*Taŋaroa).

Sit with the restored form — Tangaroa — and the diacritics themselves become the practice: each mark is a small act of attention, a refusal to let the plain ASCII form ​*tangaroa* stand in for the whole. What the tradition preserved in this name, the restoration asks the reader to preserve in turn.

## Why This Restoration Matters

Every ​stage of the journey from Polynesian transcription to Unicode was an act of care: the scribe who first wrote the name, the lexicographer who glossed it, the engineer who taught the DNS ‌to carry it. The PuniCodex restoration is the latest stage, not the last word — the Scholarly Edition is revised as the evidence improves. What does not change is the principle: a ​name deserves to be written the way its own tradition wrote it. **Tangaroa** in the address bar is that principle, made routable.

## A Closer Look at the Marks

A ‌restored name is a small map. In the case of **Tangaroa**, the map does not lead through diacritics or special letters, because the source tradition wrote the name in Polynesian transcription rather ​than in the Latin alphabet. The ASCII form *tangaroa* and the restored form share the same letters; the restoration is a decision about which conventional spelling should serve as the public reference.

‌That decision is not cosmetic. The original script attestation carries semantic and phonetic information that no romanization can fully reproduce. By fixing one conventional spelling as the canonical domain form, the project ‌prevents the drift that happens when a name is romanized differently in every article, map, and database. The breakdown still lists each character — **t**, **a**, **n**, **g**, **a**, **r**, **o**, **a** ​— so visitors can see exactly what is being carried forward and what is not. What looks like "no change" is, in fact, a deliberate choice to keep the name stable, searchable, ​and addressable.

## Tangaroa in Its Tradition

**Tangaroa** does not stand alone. It belongs to the Polynesian tradition, where it is counted among 24 names in the PuniCodex lexicon. Its sphere — Ocean, ​Sea Creatures, Fishing — places it beside other figures who govern similar aspects of experience. The restored spelling is therefore not only a philological decision; it is a way of keeping the ​name in the company of its kin. When the address bar shows **Tangaroa**, it marks the boundary between a generic search term and a named entry in a living catalog of myth. ‌That catalog is the point of the project. Every restored name is a vote for specificity: the web should know the difference between a figure and a keyword, between a tradition and ‌a trend. **Tangaroa** is one such vote.
